lead: A DAC turns an n-bit digital word into a voltage by adding binary-weighted currents at a virtual ground. The weighted-resistor network gives every bit its own resistor, which is easy to understand but needs a resistor spread of 2^(n−1) to 1, so it stops at about 4 bits. The R-2R ladder reaches 10 to 12 bits with only two resistor values, which is why it sits inside almost every DAC chip and inside every successive-approximation ADC (Chapter 7.9).
prereq: You need the inverting summing amplifier and virtual ground from Unit 6, Op-Amp Linear and Nonlinear Applications, and the offset and settling limits of real op-amps from Unit 5, Differential Amplifiers and Op-Amp Internals.

sections.h3: Weighted-resistor DAC: one resistor per bit

blocks.text: A DAC takes an n-bit word and gives a voltage proportional to its value. Write the bits b_(n−1) down to b_0, where b_(n−1) is the most significant bit (MSB) and b_0 the least significant bit (LSB). Each bit drives a switch: bit = 1 connects its resistor to V_ref, bit = 0 connects it to ground. All the resistors meet at the inverting input of an op-amp, which is a virtual ground because the non-inverting input is at 0 V. Each branch then carries a current V_ref/R_branch that does not depend on the other branches, and the op-amp adds them.

blocks.where: V_ref is the reference voltage in volts; R_f is the op-amp feedback resistor in ohms; R is the resistor of the MSB branch in ohms; b_i is the bit value, 0 or 1. The next branch uses 2R, the next 4R, and the LSB branch 2^(n−1)R.

blocks.text: The network is simple, but the resistors must be graded. The MSB branch carries V_ref/R and the LSB branch V_ref/(2^(n−1)R), a spread of 2^(n−1) to 1. The MSB resistor must also hold its value to one part in 2^n, otherwise its current alone is wrong by a whole LSB. On a chip, resistors match well only when they are identical in shape and size, so a graded set cannot be kept accurate. Weighted-resistor DACs use trimmed thin-film resistors and are impractical beyond about 4 bits.

sections.h3: R-2R ladder: two values, any number of bits

blocks.text: The ladder uses only R and 2R. A chain of series R runs from a 2R termination at the far end to the op-amp's virtual ground. At every node of the chain a 2R resistor is switched to V_ref or to ground by one bit. The bit currents add at the virtual ground and the feedback resistor R_f sets the output voltage.

The ladder works because the resistance seen looking toward the termination from any node is exactly 2R. At the last node, the 2R termination in parallel with that node's switched 2R gives R; adding the series R gives 2R again. The same step repeats node by node toward the op-amp. So the current arriving at a node splits into two equal halves, and the bit currents fall by a factor 2 at every step. Only two resistor shapes exist, repeated, so matching depends on geometry and not on absolute value.
I_i = V_ref/(2^(n−i) R)    and    V_out = −V_ref × (R_f/R) × D/2^n
blocks.where: I_i is the current that the bit in position i (i = 0 is the LSB) sends into the summing node when it is 1, in amperes; D = b_(n−1)2^(n−1) + ⋯ + b_0 is the decimal value of the input word; the rest of the symbols are as before. With R_f = R the output is simply V_out = −V_ref × D/2^n.

blocks.text: An n-bit ladder needs 2n resistors against n for the weighted network, and its settling time is set by the RC of the ladder and the switch resistances. A typical CMOS ladder settles in tens of nanoseconds and holds 10 to 12 bits.
Resolution is the number of input bits n. It fixes the step size, not the accuracy: a badly matched 12-bit part can be less accurate than a good 10-bit one.

head: Term
Meaning
rows: n bits; also the step size V_ref/2^n
time to reach within ±½ LSB of the final value
output never falls as the code rises
short spike at a code change, from unequal switch timing
shift at code 0, slope error at full scale

blocks.text: Offset error shifts the whole transfer curve and gain error tilts it; a part can have both and still be monotonic. Some systems need a swing from −V_ref/2 to +V_ref/2. Feed the ladder into a difference stage, or add a second input resistor to the summer carrying −V_ref/2. The code is then usually two's complement, 100…0 is the most negative value, and the step size stays V_ref/2^n.

figure.caption: Each bit drives its own resistor into the virtual ground; the MSB uses the smallest resistor R and every step down the word doubles it, so the current weights fall as 1, 1/2, 1/4, 1/8 and the resistor spread is 8:1 in four bits.

spec.title: Bit weights in a 4-bit weighted-resistor DAC
spec.aria: Four rows, one per bit, giving the input resistor and the fraction of the reference current that each bit contributes; the most significant bit uses the smallest resistor and the largest current.

examples.question: An 8-bit R-2R ladder DAC has V_ref = 5 V and R_f = R. The input word is 10110010. Find the decimal value D, the LSB size, the output voltage, and the largest output magnitude the DAC can produce.
steps: Write the bit weights for n = 8: b7 = 2^7 = 128, b6 = 64, b5 = 32, b4 = 16, b3 = 8, b2 = 4, b1 = 2, b0 = 1.
Read the word 1 0 1 1 0 0 1 0 from MSB to LSB. The bits that are 1 are b7, b5, b4 and b1.
The largest output comes from the all-ones word: −5 V × 255/256 = −4.9805 V, which is one LSB below V_ref in magnitude.
The sign is negative because the ladder feeds the virtual ground of an inverting summer. Add a unity-gain inverting stage if a positive output is needed.
examples.answer: D = 178, LSB = 19.53 mV, V_out = −3.4766 V, and the largest output magnitude is 4.9805 V.
examples.check:
vref = 5.0
n = 8
bits = [1, 0, 1, 1, 0, 0, 1, 0]
D = 0
for b in bits:
    D = D * 2 + b
lsb = vref / 2**n
vout = -vref * D / 2**n
vfs = vref * (2**n - 1) / 2**n
print(D)
print(round(lsb * 1000, 2))
print(round(vout, 4))
print(round(vfs, 4))

traps: Assuming the maximum output equals V_ref. Full scale is (2^n − 1)/2^n × V_ref, one LSB lower, and its sign is negative.
Dropping the minus sign. The ladder works into a virtual ground, so the op-amp inverts; a positive output needs a second inverting stage.
Confusing resolution with accuracy. Eight bits means 19.53 mV steps with V_ref = 5 V, but resistor mismatch, offset and gain error decide whether those steps are all present and in order.
Reading the word the wrong way round. 10110010 is 178 only when the leftmost bit is the MSB; read the other way it is 77.
Mixing the two denominators. The step comes from 2^n; the largest code is 2^n − 1.

quiz.q: Define resolution, LSB and full-scale output of an n-bit DAC.
quiz.a: Resolution is n bits. LSB = V_ref/2^n, the smallest output step. Full scale = V_ref(2^n − 1)/2^n, which is one LSB below V_ref.

quiz.q: Why is a weighted-resistor DAC limited to about 4 bits while an R-2R ladder reaches 12?
quiz.a: The weighted network needs resistors spanning 2^(n−1) to 1, and the MSB resistor must match to one part in 2^n, which is impossible on a chip. The ladder uses only R and 2R repeated, so matching is set by geometry and stays good as n grows.

quiz.q: Explain why the bit currents in an R-2R ladder halve at every node.
quiz.a: Looking toward the far-end termination from any node the resistance is 2R, the same as that node's switched 2R branch. The arriving current splits equally between the two, so each node passes on half and the bit currents fall as 1/2, 1/4, 1/8 …

quiz.q: A 6-bit R-2R DAC has V_ref = 8 V and R_f = R. The input word is 101101. Find D, the LSB and V_out.
A 10-bit DAC has V_ref = 10.24 V and R_f = R. Find the LSB and the full-scale output.
quiz.a: LSB = 10.24/1024 = 0.01 V = 10 mV. Full scale = −10.24 × 1023/1024 = −10.23 V, one LSB below V_ref in magnitude.

quiz.q: A DAC changes from 0111 to 1000 and the output shows a narrow spike. Explain the cause and name the two specifications involved.
quiz.a: Four bits change at once, and the switches never move at the same instant. For a short time the ladder sums a code other than 0111 or 1000, so the output spikes; this is the glitch. The time it then takes to settle within ±½ LSB of the final value is the settling time.

beyond: Not for the exam. Real audio and instrumentation DACs are segmented: a unary part of identical current sources handles the top bits, and an R-2R ladder handles the rest, which keeps both glitch and matching under control. CMOS current-steering ladders switch currents instead of voltages and settle in nanoseconds. A multiplying DAC (MDAC) lets you change V_ref on the fly, so it becomes a digitally controlled attenuator or programmable gain stage. Search for segmented DAC, current-steering DAC, INL and DNL, and MDAC.
